On 21 July 2015, a YouGov poll for _The Times_, sampling the voting intentions of current Labour Party members, projected Corbyn to win the leadership election, with 43% of first preferences and 53% of the final redistributed total.[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn_2015_Labour_Party_leadership_campaign#cite_note-100) The surge in popularity was reported to have greatly surprised even Corbyn himself.[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn_2015_Labour_Party_leadership_campaign#cite_note-101) On 11 August, _The Times_ published the results of its second YouGov poll, indicating that Corbyn was on course for a "decisive victory"; it claimed that support for Corbyn had increased further to 57% and that he would therefore win on first preferences.[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn_2015_Labour_Party_leadership_campaign#cite_note-102)_The Guardian_ reported a Survation poll showing that, after being shown a short video of all four candidates, more voters from both the wider electorate and previous Labour, Liberal Democrat and UK Independence Party (UKIP) voters indicated a preference for Corbyn.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn_2015_Labour_Party_leadership_campaign#cite_note-103)
However, on 15 August, _The Independent on Sunday_ reported a ComRes poll it had commissioned of the general public, revealing that if Corbyn were to become Labour Leader, voters believed it would reduce Labour's chances of winning the next election, whilst the election of David Miliband, who was defeated by his brother in 2010, would stand the best chance of Labour winning the next election.[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn_2015_Labour_Party_leadership_campaign#cite_note-104)

### Women-only railway carriages
Corbyn was announced to have been elected Leader of the Labour Party, at a conference held in central London, with over 59% of first-preference votes.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn_2015_Labour_Party_leadership_campaign#cite_note-Result-9) Following this result, a new group called _Momentum_ was formed. Momentum describes itself as a grassroots political advocacy group which grew out of the Jeremy Corbyn for Labour Leader campaign[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn_2015_Labour_Party_leadership_campaign#cite_note-BBC_News:_Momentum-105) which describes itself as "a network of people and organisations that will continue the energy and enthusiasm of Jeremy's campaign".[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn_2015_Labour_Party_leadership_campaign#cite_note-106) The idea was denounced by Labour critics of the leader as part of an attempt to mobilise factionally, leading to the deselection of moderate MPs and councillors "who are not judged politically correct by the veteran Bennite organisers behind Momentum".[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn_2015_Labour_Party_leadership_campaign#cite_note-107)As of October 2015 Momentum had about 60,000 supporters, charges no membership fee, organises mostly through social media and has around 50 local groups across the UK.[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn_2015_Labour_Party_leadership_campaign#cite_note-BBC_News:_Momentum-105)

### Women-only railway carriages
Labour MP and former shadow minister Emma Reynolds describes Momentum as "a parallel organisation to the Labour Party" (something which the organisation denies[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn_2015_Labour_Party_leadership_campaign#cite_note-Guardian:_Momentum-108)) and likened them to the Militant tendency.[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn_2015_Labour_Party_leadership_campaign#cite_note-BBC_News:_Momentum-105) Some hard left groups have attempted to affiliate themselves with the organisation, thus causing concern among the soft left of the Labour Party.[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn_2015_Labour_Party_leadership_campaign#cite_note-Guardian:_Momentum-108) Others on the far left have criticised the group strongly.[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn_2015_Labour_Party_leadership_campaign#cite_note-109)

Chunks: 0,1,2
The MPs who allowed Jeremy Corbyn to enter the Labour leadership contest so the party could "have a debate" are morons, according to a former adviser to Tony Blair.
Mr Corbyn, who is on course to become Labour leader according to the first public poll of those eligible to vote, scraped onto the ballot paper by winning the backing of 35 MPs - the minimum number of nominations needed to enter the race.
Some admitted nominating Mr Corbyn to ensure the contest represented the full spectrum of voices in the party and hoped members would dismiss the crazy views of the left in favour of a more mainstream candidate.
But John McTernan, who advised Mr Blair during his time as Prime Minister, blamed them for the "disastrous" poll, which gave Mr Corbyn an astonishing 17 per cent lead over the second-placed candidate, Andy Burnham.
In a blistering attack, Mr McTernan told BBC Two _Newsnight:_ “The moronic MPs who nominated Jeremy Corbyn to ‘have a debate’ need their heads felt. They should be ashamed of themselves. They’re morons.”

The MPs who allowed Jeremy Corbyn to enter the Labour leadership contest so the party could "have a debate" are morons, according to a former adviser to Tony Blair.
Mr Corbyn, who is on course to become Labour leader according to the first public poll of those eligible to vote, scraped onto the ballot paper by winning the backing of 35 MPs - the minimum number of nominations needed to enter the race.
Some admitted nominating Mr Corbyn to ensure the contest represented the full spectrum of voices in the party and hoped members would dismiss the crazy views of the left in favour of a more mainstream candidate.
But John McTernan, who advised Mr Blair during his time as Prime Minister, blamed them for the "disastrous" poll, which gave Mr Corbyn an astonishing 17 per cent lead over the second-placed candidate, Andy Burnham.
In a blistering attack, Mr McTernan told BBC Two _Newsnight:_ “The moronic MPs who nominated Jeremy Corbyn to ‘have a debate’ need their heads felt. They should be ashamed of themselves. They’re morons.”
So who were the 35 MPs?

On 21 July 2015, a YouGov poll for _The Times_, sampling the voting intentions of current Labour Party members, projected Corbyn to win the leadership election, with 43% of first preferences and 53% of the final redistributed total.[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn_2015_Labour_Party_leadership_campaign#cite_note-100) The surge in popularity was reported to have greatly surprised even Corbyn himself.[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn_2015_Labour_Party_leadership_campaign#cite_note-101) On 11 August, _The Times_ published the results of its second YouGov poll, indicating that Corbyn was on course for a "decisive victory"; it claimed that support for Corbyn had increased further to 57% and that he would therefore win on first preferences.[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn_2015_Labour_Party_leadership_campaign#cite_note-102)_The Guardian_ reported a Survation poll showing that, after being shown a short video of all four candidates, more voters from both the wider electorate and previous Labour, Liberal Democrat and UK Independence Party (UKIP) voters indicated a preference for Corbyn.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn_2015_Labour_Party_leadership_campaign#cite_note-103)
However, on 15 August, _The Independent on Sunday_ reported a ComRes poll it had commissioned of the general public, revealing that if Corbyn were to become Labour Leader, voters believed it would reduce Labour's chances of winning the next election, whilst the election of David Miliband, who was defeated by his brother in 2010, would stand the best chance of Labour winning the next election.[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn_2015_Labour_Party_leadership_campaign#cite_note-104)

Labour leadership candidates need nominations from 10% of MP and MEPs in their party – a total of 22 – in order to progress to the next stage of the election. Each Labour MP has received nomination papers and those choosing to participate must cast their vote by 2.30pm on Monday, January 13th.
Candidates are allowed to nominate themselves and this will contribute to their total number of nominations. Nominations are valid once submitted unless the candidate in question formally withdraws from the race by writing to Labour’s general secretary. Those who have nominated the MP who has withdrawn can then submit a new nomination (before the deadline).
Those candidates who secure enough nominations to enter the second stage of the contest will then have to gain nominations from either 5% of local parties – 33 – or 5% of affiliated members including three affiliated organisations of which two must be trade unions. If candidates meet both of these requirements, they will be included on the ballot paper.
Rebecca Long-Bailey, Lisa Nandy, Jess Phillips and Keir Starmer all reached the threshold for MP/MEP nominations, and Emily Thornberry eventually scraped through too. Clive Lewis withdrew from the race.

Five candidates have made it through to the next stage where they will battle it out to become the next Labour leader after a dramatic late show of support saw Emily Thornberry scrape through.
Rebecca Long-Bailey, Lisa Nandy and Jess Phillips had already secured enough nominations to continue to the next stage of the Labour leadership election, as well as early front-runner Sir Keir Starmer.
And after Clive Lewis announced he would withdraw to allow his supporters to nominate other contenders, Ms Thornberry secured just enough votes to get through to the next round.
Barry Gardiner, who was a late and brief entrant to the race, had already pulled out after failing to receive any nominations.
Candidates need nominations from 10 per cent of Labour MPs and MEPs – thee equivalent of 22.
The timetable for the three month leadership contest, agreed by the NEC on Monday, states nominations from MPs and MEPs are open until Monday, after which nominations from CLPs and party affiliates open.

Labour leadership candidates need nominations from 10% of MP and MEPs in their party – a total of 22 – in order to progress to the next stage of the election. Each Labour MP has received nomination papers and those choosing to participate must cast their vote by 2.30pm on Monday, January 13th.
Candidates are allowed to nominate themselves and this will contribute to their total number of nominations. Nominations are valid once submitted unless the candidate in question formally withdraws from the race by writing to Labour’s general secretary. Those who have nominated the MP who has withdrawn can then submit a new nomination (before the deadline).
Those candidates who secure enough nominations to enter the second stage of the contest will then have to gain nominations from either 5% of local parties – 33 – or 5% of affiliated members including three affiliated organisations of which two must be trade unions. If candidates meet both of these requirements, they will be included on the ballot paper.
Rebecca Long-Bailey, Lisa Nandy, Jess Phillips and Keir Starmer all reached the threshold for MP/MEP nominations, and Emily Thornberry eventually scraped through too. Clive Lewis withdrew from the race.

Five candidates have made it through to the next stage where they will battle it out to become the next Labour leader after a dramatic late show of support saw Emily Thornberry scrape through.
Rebecca Long-Bailey, Lisa Nandy and Jess Phillips had already secured enough nominations to continue to the next stage of the Labour leadership election, as well as early front-runner Sir Keir Starmer.
And after Clive Lewis announced he would withdraw to allow his supporters to nominate other contenders, Ms Thornberry secured just enough votes to get through to the next round.
Barry Gardiner, who was a late and brief entrant to the race, had already pulled out after failing to receive any nominations.
Candidates need nominations from 10 per cent of Labour MPs and MEPs – thee equivalent of 22.
The timetable for the three month leadership contest, agreed by the NEC on Monday, states nominations from MPs and MEPs are open until Monday, after which nominations from CLPs and party affiliates open.
